title: From the street to the Olympics
short: From the street to the Olympics
text: On a hot afternoon in July 2021, a thirteen-year-old girl from Japan called Momiji Nishiya stepped onto the podium in Tokyo to receive an Olympic gold medal. Beside her stood the silver medallist, Rayssa Leal from Brazil, who was also thirteen. It was the first time skateboarding had ever been included in the Olympic Games, and the youngest athletes in the competition had just made history. For many people watching around the world, it was a sign of how much the sport had changed.

Skateboarding was born in California in the nineteen fifties, when surfers began attaching wheels to wooden boards so that they could practise their moves on land when the waves were too small. For several decades, it was seen as a hobby for rebellious teenagers rather than a serious sport. Skaters were often chased out of car parks and shopping centres, and in some cities skateboarding in public places was even banned.

Yet the culture kept growing. Skaters invented new tricks, built their own ramps and filmed each other, creating a style that was as much about creativity and self-expression as about competition. Unlike many traditional sports, there were no coaches, no official rules and no fixed way of doing things. What mattered was originality, and the respect of other skaters.

When the International Olympic Committee announced in 2016 that skateboarding would be part of the Tokyo Games, the reaction was mixed. Some skaters were delighted, seeing it as recognition of decades of hard work and a chance to inspire a new generation. Others were deeply suspicious. They feared that the Olympics would turn skateboarding into just another sport, with judges, uniforms and strict training programmes, and that its free spirit would be lost.

In the end, many of those fears proved to be exaggerated. The competitions in Tokyo were relaxed and friendly, and the athletes often celebrated the best tricks of their rivals. Spectators were particularly struck by the support the skaters gave each other. After one competitor fell on her final attempt, the others lifted her onto their shoulders. For some commentators, this spirit was a refreshing contrast to the intense rivalry seen in many other sports.

The Games also had a practical impact. In several countries, the number of young people taking up skateboarding rose sharply after the Olympics, and many cities began to build new skateparks. Girls in particular seemed to be inspired by seeing athletes of their own age on the podium. Sky Brown, who won a bronze medal for Great Britain at the age of thirteen, became a role model for thousands of children.

Of course, the debate has not completely disappeared. Some skaters still believe that the true heart of skateboarding is on the street, not in a stadium. But perhaps the two can exist side by side. After all, every Olympic champion started in the same way: with a board, a bit of concrete and the courage to fall and try again.
q: What made the event in Tokyo historic?
It was the first time a teenager had competed in the Olympics.
It was the first Olympic skateboarding competition, with very young medallists.
It was the first competition between Japan and Brazil.
It was the first time Japan had won a gold medal.
It was invented as a new Olympic sport.
Surfers wanted a way to practise when they could not surf.
Teenagers wanted a new way to travel to school.
According to the third paragraph, what was most important in skateboarding culture?
following the instructions of a good coach
being original and earning the respect of other skaters
Why were some skaters suspicious of the Olympics?
They were afraid skateboarding would lose its free spirit.
They believed skateboarding was too dangerous.
They did not want to wear medals.
They thought the Games were too far away.
What impressed spectators most in Tokyo?
the way the skaters supported each other
the strict behaviour of the judges
the difficulty of the final tricks
the number of skaters who fell
What does the writer suggest in the last paragraph?
Skaters should stop arguing and leave the Olympics.
Only street skaters are real skaters.
Olympic skating will soon replace street skating.
Street skating and Olympic skating can both have a place.
In which paragraph does the writer mention changes in the number of people who skate?
In which paragraph does the writer describe how skaters were treated in the past?
In which paragraph does the writer describe a kind gesture towards a competitor?
In which paragraph does the writer mention when the decision about the Olympics was announced?
